title: BLAKE (hash function)
text:
BLAKE3 is a cryptographic hash function based on Bao and BLAKE2, created by Jack O'Connor, Jean-Philippe Aumasson, Samuel Neves, and Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn.[1] It was announced on January 9, 2020, at Real World Crypto.[2]

BLAKE3 is a single algorithm with many desirable features (parallelism, XOF, KDF, PRF and MAC), in contrast to BLAKE and BLAKE2, which are algorithm families with multiple variants. BLAKE3 has a binary tree structure, so it supports a practically unlimited degree of parallelism (both SIMD and multithreading) given long enough input. The official Rust and C implementations[3] are dual-licensed as public domain (CC0) and the Apache License.[4]

BLAKE3 is designed to be as fast as possible. It is consistently a few times faster than BLAKE2. The BLAKE3 compression function is closely based on that of BLAKE2s, with the biggest difference being that the number of rounds is reduced from 10 to 7, a change based on an argument that past cryptography is too conservative compared to current cryptoanalysis records.[5] In addition to providing parallelism, the Merkle tree format also allows for verified streaming (on-the-fly verifying) and incremental updates.[3]

### Users of BLAKE3

Bazel build system supports using BLAKE3 as a file digest function.[6]

Ccache uses it for its hash function.[7]

ClickHouse has it as dependency.[8]

Total Commander supports BLAKE3 for file checksums.

IPFS again has support for BLAKE3 hashes.[9]

OpenZFS supports BLAKE3 from version 2.2

Cargo (Rust) uses BLAKE3 for checksums.[10]

Czkawka files janitor https://github.com/qarmin/czkawka

LLVM has introduced BLAKE3 implementation.[11]

Wasmer a WebAssembly runtime that uses BLAKE3 hashing.[12]

Software bill of material software CycloneDX uses it as part of its suite of hash functions.[13]

Mosaic uses BLAKE3 instead of SHA-512 (SHA-2) for its Ed25519 signature.[14]

Epic games Lore version control system uses BLAKE3 for its address function.[15]
